result: Deletion of mreB from P. fluorescens SBW25 results in viable spherical cells with variable volume and reduced fitness. The ΔmreB cells are larger and more variable in volume than ancestral cells, have reduced viability (81% vs 95%), and show longer generation time, extended lag phase, and lower maximum yield.
evaluation: All three reviewers explicitly acknowledge this finding. Reviewer 1 states the work shows 'how a genetic lesion in MreB that causes rod-shaped cells to become spherical, with concomitant deleterious fitness effects, can be rescued.' Reviewer 3 notes 'The loss of fitness associated with MreB deletion causes high variation in cell volume among sibling cells after cell division' as a leading result. No concerns are raised about these basic characterization data.

result: Reduced fitness of ΔmreB cells arises primarily from differential growth of daughter cells. The accuracy of septum positioning is altered (19.4% vs 5% difference in sister cell volumes), but more importantly, elongation rates differ by 55% between sister cells in ΔmreB vs only 5% in wild-type. This growth asymmetry is identified as the primary cause of cell volume variability.
evaluation: Reviewer 3 explicitly lists this as a leading result: 'The loss of fitness associated with MreB deletion causes high variation in cell volume among sibling cells after cell division.' The detailed mechanistic investigation using time-resolved microscopy is praised by Reviewer 1 as part of the 'convincing evolution experiments with molecular and genetic techniques.' No reviewer questions these single-cell measurements or their interpretation.

result: A 1000-generation selection experiment resulted in rapid restoration of fitness with derived cells retaining spherical shape. Fitness was restored to wild-type levels by generation 250, with highly similar trajectories across all 10 replicate populations. All evolved lines remained spherical (coccoid).
evaluation: All reviewers explicitly acknowledge this key finding. Reviewer 2 notes 'the finding that the round phenotype was maintained during evolution rather than that the original phenotype, rod shape cells, was recovered is interesting.' Reviewer 3 states 'The answer is no. The evolved lineages recovered fitness by the end of the experiment, growing just as well as the unevolved rod-shaped ancestor, but remained spherical.' The rapid and parallel nature of compensation is not questioned.

result: Mutations in pbp1A were identified as the main route for evolutionary rescue. Seven of ten independent lines had pbp1A mutations, with specific mutations identified (D484N, D721A, T362P, N698K). Sequencing at generation 50 showed all lines had at least one pbp1A mutation, demonstrating the relative ease at which these mutations arise.
evaluation: Reviewer 3 explicitly lists this as a leading result: 'Fitness recovery is largely driven by a single, loss-of-function point mutation that evolves within the first ~250 generations.' Reviewer 1 notes the work combines 'convincing evolution experiments with molecular and genetic techniques' and that 'genetic reconstruction experiments confirmed...that single point mutations reducing or eliminating pbp1A gene function were sufficient.' No concerns are raised about the sequencing or genetic reconstruction data.

result: Compensatory pbp1A mutations restored fitness and cell size homeostasis. Genetic reconstructions of pbp1A mutations (D484N and T362P) in the ΔmreB background produced cells with near-ancestral volume and fitness. Loss-of-function of pbp1A (via deletion) was sufficient to restore fitness, demonstrating these are loss-of-function mutations.
evaluation: Reviewer 1 states 'genetic reconstruction experiments confirmed, particularly for the class of mutant with defects in pbp1A, that single point mutations reducing or eliminating gene function were sufficient.' Reviewer 3 notes the work provides 'an impressively detailed investigation of the genetic and molecular changes that evolved' with no concerns raised about the reconstruction experiments or their interpretation.

result: Evolved lines restored cell size homeostasis by balancing elongation and septation rates and reducing growth asymmetry between daughter cells. All evolved lines regained symmetry in elongation rate (most notably) and septum positioning. The improvement in elongation rate symmetry correlates directly with increased probability that daughter cells are viable.
evaluation: Reviewer 3 explicitly states 'Fitness recovery is largely driven by a single, loss-of-function point mutation that evolves within the first ~250 generations that reduces the variability in cell volume among siblings.' Reviewer 1 notes the work 'increases our understanding of how mreB contributes to cell wall synthesis and shows how compensatory mutations may reestablish its homogeneity.' The detailed single-cell analysis is not questioned by any reviewer.

result: ΔmreB cells showed increased peptidoglycan cross-linking (40.47% vs 36.34% in wild-type), likely from enhanced TPase activity of Pbp1A. The pbp1A mutants in both backgrounds showed lower cross-linking (31-34%), suggesting mutations decreased transpeptidation or increased transglycosylation. Bocillin-FL labeling confirmed elevated Pbp1A activity in ΔmreB cells.
evaluation: Reviewer 3 explicitly lists as a leading result: 'The main route to restoring fitness and reducing variability involves loss of function mutations causing a reduction of TPase and peptidoglycan cross-linking, leading to a disorganized cell wall architecture characteristic of spherical cells.' Reviewer 1 notes the work 'shows how compensatory mutations may reestablish its homogeneity' with reference to cell wall synthesis. The biochemical data are not questioned.

result: Cell wall synthesis patterns differ between ΔmreB P. fluorescens and MreB-depleted E. coli. In ΔmreB SBW25, BADA labeling was heterogeneous across the cell wall, contrary to the diffuse and homogeneous synthesis observed in E. coli. The pbp1A mutations restored more homogeneous synthesis focused at the septal region.
evaluation: Reviewer 1 explicitly states the work 'increases our understanding of how mreB contributes to cell wall synthesis and shows how compensatory mutations may reestablish its homogeneity.' The FDAA labeling data showing heterogeneous synthesis in ΔmreB and restoration of homogeneity in evolved lines is part of the 'impressively detailed investigation' praised by Reviewer 3. No concerns are raised about these observations.

result: Alternative evolutionary routes to fitness restoration were identified in three lines without pbp1A mutations. Line 2 had an ftsA mutation, Line 5 had an ftsZ mutation, and Line 7 had a five-gene deletion including oprD plus a later ftsE mutation. The Line 7 deletion restored fitness but with extended lag time and some septation defects.
evaluation: Reviewer 3 acknowledges 'Fitness recovery is largely driven by a single, loss-of-function point mutation' but does not question the alternative routes. The comprehensive sequencing and characterization of all lines is part of the 'impressively detailed investigation' noted by Reviewer 3. No reviewer raises concerns about these alternative evolutionary paths or their characterization.

result: When pbp1A mutations were reconstructed in ancestral SBW25, they had little effect on population dynamics or shape but reduced elongation rates and produced narrower cells with smaller volumes. This suggests the mutations result in reduction or complete loss-of-function of Pbp1A.
evaluation: This is part of the genetic reconstruction experiments that Reviewer 1 notes 'confirmed...that single point mutations reducing or eliminating pbp1A gene function were sufficient.' The characterization of effects in the wild-type background is part of demonstrating these are loss-of-function mutations, which is not questioned by any reviewer.

result: During exponential phase, the elongation rate of ΔmreB cells was indistinguishable from wild-type, but cell volume rapidly decreased. The added volumes of evolved spherical cells matched theoretical predictions for passage from cylindrical to spherical geometry with constant turgor pressure, suggesting adaptive mutations restored mechanical integrity of the cell wall.
evaluation: This biophysical analysis is part of the 'impressively detailed investigation' praised by Reviewer 3. The combination of experimental measurements with theoretical predictions is not questioned. Reviewer 1 notes the work 'increases our understanding of how mreB contributes to cell wall synthesis,' which encompasses these mechanistic insights.

result: DNA content scaled with cell volume in both wild-type and ΔmreB cells. The largest ΔmreB cells had many times the DNA content of ancestral cells. Evolved lines and reconstructed mutants showed reduced cell volumes that correlated with reduced DNA content compared to the ΔmreB ancestor.
evaluation: This is part of the comprehensive characterization of cell physiology that is not questioned by any reviewer. The flow cytometry data supporting these claims are part of the 'various different techniques' noted by Reviewer 2 as a strength of the paper.

result: ΔmreB cells appear spherical but have an elongation axis that remains constant throughout the cell cycle, with the septum forming perpendicularly to this axis. After division, the elongation axis rotates 90° relative to the mother cell, reminiscent of ovococci. This pattern is maintained in evolved lines.
evaluation: This detailed characterization of cell division patterns is part of the time-resolved microscopy analysis that supports the main findings. It is not questioned by any reviewer and contributes to understanding how spherical cells maintain organized division despite loss of MreB.
